sources.claim: For federal income tax, a single-member LLC is by default disregarded (taxed with its owner) and a multi-member LLC is by default a partnership; an LLC can elect to be taxed as a corporation.

sections.skill: Separate legal form from tax treatment

questions.prompt: Who sets a business's legal form?

choices.text: The IRS, by assigning it a tax form
State law, through the entity's formation
The bank, when it opens an account

questions.correct_answer: State law, through the entity's formation
questions.intro: A business's LEGAL FORM (sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, corporation) is set by state law. Its TAX TREATMENT is how the IRS taxes it, which is a separate question. An LLC is a good example. By default, for federal income tax, a single-owner LLC is usually taxed with its owner (the IRS calls it "disregarded"), and a multi-owner LLC is usually taxed as a partnership. An LLC can choose (elect) to be taxed as a corporation. So "LLC" tells you the legal form, not automatically how it is taxed. Source: IRS; check current rules.
questions.feedback: Legal form comes from state law.

questions.prompt: A business's legal form is like a student's what?
questions.intro: Think of a student with two labels: the school they attend (set by enrollment) and the sports team they play on (set by tryouts). Knowing the school does not tell you the team. A business also has two labels: its legal form (set by state filings) and its tax treatment (set by IRS rules and elections). Knowing one does not automatically tell you the other.
